title: Learning Treatment Allocations with Risk Control Under Partial Identifiability
claim: The tolerance parameter trades off two risks: loosening it raises treatment risk toward the bound while lowering overall population risk.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots sharing x-axis, shaded quantile bands, dashed diagonal bound
description: Two side-by-side line plots, labeled (a) and (b), share the same x-axis: tolerance tau from 0% to 40%. Each shows a blue mean curve with circle markers and a light-blue shaded band for the 10–90th percentile across 1000 datasets. Panel (a) plots treatment risk P(L=1|A=1) on the y-axis from 0% to 40%. The curve rises with tau and stays below a dashed black diagonal, the tolerance bound, then plateaus near 25% after tau of 35%. Panel (b) plots population risk P(L=1) from 0% to 100%. The curve falls from about 77% at tau of 5% to a plateau near 25%. The band is widest at small tau. A legend in panel (a) labels the mean and the quantile band. Grey gridlines frame both plots.
caption: Tolerance $\trt$ versus (a) treatment risk and (b) population risk of learned allocation policies $\policy$. The proposed learning method is set to limit the treatment risk to be no greater than $\trt$ with a probability of at least $90%$. The shaded regions (10-90th percentiles) represent the resulting risks of policies learned from 1000 different datasets. Thus $\trt$ trades off two types of risks (a) and (b). The details of the example are given in [ref].
abstract: Learning beneficial treatment allocations for a patient population is an important problem in precision medicine. Many treatments come with adverse side effects that are not commensurable with their potential benefits. Patients who do not receive benefits after such treatments are thereby subjected to unnecessary harm. This is a `treatment risk' that we aim to control when learning beneficial allocations. The constrained learning problem is challenged by the fact that the treatment risk is not in general identifiable using either randomized trial or observational data. We propose a certifiable learning method that controls the treatment risk with finite samples in the partially identified setting. The method is illustrated using both simulated and real data.
